title: Because you have the cursed jesuit strain in you, only it’s injected the wrong way.
html_source: Stephen, like the real James Joyce, had much of his schooling at institutions run by the Society of Jesus, a Catholic order better known as the Jesuits: first at the Clongowes primary school and then at Belvedere College secondary school. Stephen was strongly influenced by his Jesuit education which combines rigorous Aristotelian scholasticism with strict Catholic zeal, as is depicted in Joyce’s previous novel A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man. Stephen can’t help thinking in a Jesuit-influenced way even years after he left the church and renounced the Catholic concept of God. Hence Buck claiming that Stephen still has the “jesuit strain” in him, only it goes “the wrong way”: Stephen uses Catholic reasoning to formulate his opposition to Catholicism. Many of his thoughts throughout the book reference thinkers who are key parts of a Jesuit curriculum: Aristotle, St. Thomas Aquinas, and Jesuits founder St. Ignatius of Loyola (whom Mulligan encourages Stephen to “chuck” a few lines later). Stephen’s anxieties sometimes turn to Catholic conceptions of hellfire and damnation; in chapter 10, “Wandering Rocks”, Mulligan suggests this comes from his education by Jesuits who “drove his wits astray [by] visions of hell”, which is why “he can never be a poet”.

anchor.text: Because you have the cursed jesuit strain in you, only it's injected the wrong way.
anchor.prefix: es in the dissectingroom. It's a beastly thing and nothing else. It simply doesn't matter. You wouldn't kneel down to pray for your mother on her deathbed when she asked you. Why?
anchor.suffix: To me it's all a mockery and beastly. Her cerebral lobes are not functioning. She calls the doctor sir Peter Teazle and picks buttercups off the quilt. Humour her till it's over.
